blocks.p: The safety state is at the top of the Polyvagal ladder. Myelinated fibers send safety signals from the brainstem to the body through the ventral vagus. These come from the nucleus ambiguus of the brainstem (but that's probably more than you need to know). The safety state is one of two parasympathetic systems and is the evolutionarily newest.

Feeling safe and connected with others comes from activating the safety state. In humans and other mammals, social engagement behaviors also contribute to this feeling. We all share some level of ability to connect and build families and herds, tribes, or even cities.

This state is imperative for mammals' general health and wellness. When we exist in this state, our bodies utilize resources for "health, growth, and restoration," as Dr. Porges often says. Our bodies function better, are healthier, and meet developmental milestones. We form attachments and relationships with healthy boundaries. We just generally experience more goodness and live more fulfilling lives.
These are some examples of what being in the safe/social state can feel like:

The safety state generally feels like connection: to others, the self, or the environment. We are more attuned to our senses, our internal feelings, and the emotions of others. We're curious and open to what the present moment brings, and not fearful and evaluative.

Life is manageable when we are in this state. Not perfect, but manageable. Life doesn't feel as overwhelming, tense, or pressured. When we face problems, which we will (sorry), we can navigate them more easily. We can navigate them using negotiation and cooperation and not panic or overwhelm. We compromise but don't sacrifice. We don't relinquish our power, dignity, or purpose for the selfish needs of another.

We can better detect safety or danger cues from the safety state. We can identify red flags more accurately when around someone giving off danger cues. If we retain our access to our safety pathways in these moments, we can potentially navigate the situation and ameliorate it by providing our own cues of safety to the other person.

Along with changes in emotion and feeling, this state also brings cognitive changes. In this state, we can focus, plan, think, learn, assess, and weigh the pros and cons. We have greater access to our executive functioning, something critical for students to learn and succeed academically. Increased executive functioning can also help when considering a new career, new life path, or a significant purchase. These cognitive skills are necessary for daily functioning of all types.

You can tell when someone is accessing their safety state by looking at their body language and face. Someone in this state will utilize their face and neck muscles. When they listen, their head may tilt to one side, and crinkles will form around their eyes as they squint. They can't do so without these biological pathways activated: at least, not genuinely.

When you feel safe and connected, you make and sustain eye contact. Conversely, when you feel uncomfortable, you look away. Often, in therapy, a client will have difficulty sustaining eye contact. But they make fleeting eye contact as they gain more access to their safety pathways. They look up at the therapist and then look away, darting their eyes back and forth. As they gain familiarity with these feelings of safety, they sustain eye contact for more extended periods.

When the safety pathways are active, the inner ear muscles allow a greater range of mammalian voice, something called "vocal prosody." Human beings hear each other better. We even tune out other noises and focus on the prosody in someone else's voice. Think about being at a concert or some other crowded venue: you can hear the person you're with because you're attuned to hearing mammalian voices and can tune out the background noises.

Mammals are also capable of using vocal prosody from the safety state: the sing-songy quality of voice. Mammals can use their voice to indicate a greater range of emotions and intentions. We can raise our voices to show excitement and lower our voices to show seriousness. When you speak from safety, your expression is more ranged. When you speak from danger, your voice is restricted and monotone.

Another obvious indicator that someone is in their state of safety is that they can spontaneously get closer to others and use appropriate touch. Think about the first time you saw someone you care about after coming out of quarantine in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. You probably felt a spontaneous impulse to hug them, right? When you see someone you love, you probably hug or kiss them when you greet each other. Or just shake hands with someone new or someone you have some appreciation for.

Someone in their safety state can use a broader range of physical gestures. Their bodies are more animated, and they can express themselves more freely. Dance is fun, as is physical exercise with another person.
There are other physiological changes when in safety:

Nobody exists in a pure safety state. Generally, anyone can activate these pathways and feel them on some level. It may be a significant challenge, but it is possible. Even someone with a substantial history of surviving severe traumatic events can eventually access these pathways with safe enough environments and safe enough people around them.

Again, no one exists entirely in these states, but we don't need to. We need enough access to these biological pathways to feel safe and benefit from their biological functions. When the safety state is active, defensive activation won't be out of control. Anxiety, depression, anger, and more reduce in their intensity and frequency.

So, the more access we have to the safety states, the better. Big and small events in life, even in a single day, will constantly challenge our ability to exist in the safety state. That's not going to change. However, what can change is how much access we have to the state and how exercised those pathways are.

When we discuss what's needed to feel safe, we're talking about what is required to activate the safety biology. Two major components are the environment and the people in our lives. These provide potential neuroceptions of safety and help the individual climb their Polyvagal ladder.

The environment does not need to be perfect to achieve a state of safety. For instance, even in a dangerous neighborhood surrounding a school, students can potentially access this state, especially when the school staff are in their own safety states. One can still smile and hold hands with their loved one in a crowded mall on Christmas Eve.

Safe people and safe environments provide passive safety neuroceptions. You detect their safety cues without conscious awareness or control. However, you can also actively access safety through mindfulness of the present moment, singing, dancing, and other forms of creativity.

blocks.why: Safety can be accessed on purpose, not only waited for. This practice does that, tuned to you.

blocks.prompt: Can you identify one moment in the past week when you were in your safety state? How could you tell?
When was the last time you made eye contact with a pet or person and were okay with it? Who were you with? What felt okay about it?
When did you last smile? What was happening?
What passive safety cues are in your life? (Think of people and places.)
What can you actively do to feel safe?
How often do you feel safe in a week?
What is one obstacle to safety that you can change? Is there something you can change in your environment? Is there an activity you can set up for yourself? Is there a sensory cue you can set up?

q: "Operationally defining feelings of safety as dependent on an autonomic state, provides an opportunity to study the potential emergent properties that are dependent on access to this state. Thus, it is proposed that the consequence of feeling safe provides the neural platform for cooperative behaviors, both supporting physiological systems and enabling accessibility to higher brain structures for learning, creativity, appreciation of aesthetics, and even spirituality." (Porges)

blocks.p: My translation: Feeling safe depends on our body's automatic state. When in safety, we can do really cool human things using big brain power.

q: "...the Polyvagal Theory provides a neurobiological model to explain how positive social behavior, social support and positive affective states might support health and growth. In contrast to the health-related states associated with prosocial behavior, withdrawal of this new neural system would promote mobilization behaviors such as fight and flight as well as other physiological responses (e.g., increased sympathetic activity and activation of the HPA axis) that may be potentially damaging if maintained for prolonged periods. Thus, it is possible that individuals with specific psychiatric disorders, in which compromised social behavior is a diagnostic feature, are experiencing neurophysiological states that foster defensive and not social behaviors." (Porges)

blocks.p: My translation: Positive social interactions are good. Without these, our body shifts to fight-or-flight, which is bad if it lasts too long. This may explain why people with mental health disorders struggle with socializing.
